Definition: Whether government taxes, customs duties, and other revenue can be paid using the instant digital payment system, indicating integration of payment infrastructure with tax administration systems.
Comments: Guinea launched “Trésor Pay” (rolled out 22 Dec 2025) as a digital platform to dematerialize payment of administrative fees and charges owed to the state, using electronic money services—evidence of active digital revenue collection ([We are Tech](https://www.wearetech.africa/en/fils-uk/news/finance/guinea-rolls-out-tresor-pay-as-digital-gateway-for-public-payments)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed and strengthened beyond the single Trésor Pay source. Guinea's DGI operates the eTax portal (mandatory for registered taxpayers since Jan 2021) for online tax declaration and e-payment (VAT, corporate/income tax), and the GUCEG single window offers electronic payment of customs duties and fees; Trésor Pay (Dec 2025) digitises non-tax administrative fees, and Orange Money has processed vehicle tax payments since 2017. Together these corroborate "Yes" (3) across tax, customs and other revenue streams, not just one platform.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system supports business payments to suppliers, vendors, contractors, and other businesses for commercial transactions, procurement, and supply chain payments.
Comments: B2B payments are supported at least through bank transfer rails: BCRG describes RTGS for large-value interbank payments and bank transfers used for inter-enterprise transactions (“transactions interentreprises”), indicating availability of business digital transfers ([BCRG – Les systèmes et moyens de paiement](https://www.bcrg-guinee.org/les-systemes-et-moyens-de-paiement-en-republique-de-guinee/)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. A second, fresher source corroborates: the Dec 2025 Orange Money–BCI "Accès à ma banque" interoperability service is explicitly described by its operator as facilitating B2B transactions for wholesalers (grossistes), in addition to the existing bank-transfer rail for inter-enterprise payments described by BCRG. Code 2 (Yes) confirmed.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system is used or can be used for government disbursements to citizens, including social transfers, welfare payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies, grants, and emergency assistance.
Comments: Evidence indicates limited G2P usage through mobile money: GSMA documents Orange Money Guinea processing “disbursements of university scholarships for students via mobile money” (a government/education disbursement use case), but no evidence found of broad nationwide digitized social transfer programs ([GSMA Mobile for Development](https://www.gsma.com/solutions-and-impact/connectivity-for-good/mobile-for-development/programme/mobile-money/making-debut-p2g-payments-orange-money-collaborates-government-ease-vehicle-tax-collections-guinea/)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The cited GSMA source does NOT support the stated claim — it is about vehicle-tax P2G payments and makes no mention of scholarship disbursements; the original comment appears to misattribute content. Independent evidence still supports "Limited Use": a Dec 2023 circular ordered civil servants onto bank-transfer salary payment, but a 2024 report shows the transition was incomplete and error-prone (months of unpaid salaries); the Nov 2025 FUGAS platform centralises payroll/HR data but is an administrative system, not itself a disbursement rail; and BCRG's Dec 2025 instant-payment announcement states G2P digitisation is still a forward objective. Code retained at 2 (Limited Use) but on corrected sourcing — original citation should be disregarded.

Definition: Whether the system enables citizen payments to government for taxes, fees, licenses, fines, utility bills, and other government service charges.
Comments: Orange Money Guinea implemented person-to-government (P2G) payments for motor vehicle tax collections (road tax), launched March 2017, enabling users to pay via mobile money (“Pay Tax” option) with reconciliation to the Treasury ([GSMA Mobile for Development](https://www.gsma.com/solutions-and-impact/connectivity-for-good/mobile-for-development/programme/mobile-money/making-debut-p2g-payments-orange-money-collaborates-government-ease-vehicle-tax-collections-guinea/)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed and substantially strengthened. The 2017 GSMA vehicle-tax example is verified as described, and is now corroborated by the much fresher Trésor Pay platform (launched 22 Dec 2025), which lets citizens pay for passports, national ID cards, driving licences and birth certificates via mobile phone. Code 3 (Yes – Active Use) confirmed with stronger, current evidence.

Definition: Whether and how the central bank participates in payment system governance beyond its regulatory oversight role, including board representation, operational management, technical standard-setting, or direct system operation.
Comments: BCRG directly operates core payment infrastructures through its DSMP (Direction des Systèmes et Moyens de Paiement): DSMP “garantir le bon fonctionnement du système RTGS” and “assurer le fonctionnement continu des systèmes de compensation,” including daily operational management, incident handling, and statistics—showing direct central bank operation rather than only regulation ([BCRG – Rôle et Mission de la DSMP](https://www.bcrg-guinee.org/role-et-mission-de-la-dsmp/)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. BCRG's DSMP directly runs day-to-day RTGS and ACH/ACP operations (start/close of settlement days, incident resolution, reconciliation) — this is direct operation, not mere regulation. Note for context: the newer national Switch/instant-payment project is run by Guinéenne de Monétique (GuiM), a private economic-interest grouping in which BCRG is a founding member with board representation, rather than being directly BCRG-operated — but this does not alter the score for the legacy RTGS/ACH systems, which remain directly BCRG-run. Code 5 confirmed.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: Guinea’s electronic transactions law (Loi L/2016/035/AN) includes consumer protection elements for electronic transactions (e.g., requiring clear information on prices/contract terms for online transactions), but no dedicated payments consumer protection regime (e.g., e-money disputes/chargebacks) was identified in the reviewed materials—so scored as partial ([ANSSI Guinée – Loi L/2016/035/AN](https://anssi.gov.gn/?nproject=loi-l035-2016-relative-aux-transactions-electroniques)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. BCRG's published payment-system regulatory instruments (RTGS settlement instruction, ACH/clearing rules) are operational/technical, not consumer-protection focused, and no dedicated e-money consumer protection regulation was found. A Feb 2026 e-money withdrawal crisis was resolved through ad hoc negotiation between BCRG and a consumer-defence association rather than through a pre-existing formal payments consumer protection framework, reinforcing the "Partial" (general law only, reactive practice) characterisation. Code 2 confirmed.

Definition: Whether national data protection or privacy legislation exists and explicitly covers payment transaction data, including provisions on data collection, storage, sharing, retention, and user rights over their payment data.
Comments: Guinea has general personal data protection legislation via Law L/2016/037/AN on cybersecurity and protection of personal data, published by Guinea’s national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI), which establishes a legal framework for personal data protection (not payment-specific provisions identified) ([ANSSI Guinée – Loi L/2016/037/AN](https://anssi.gov.gn/?nproject=loi-l037-2016-relative-a-la-cybersecurite-et-la-protection-des-donnees-a-caractere-personnel)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Loi L/2016/037/AN establishes a general cybersecurity and personal-data-protection framework covering all sectors; no payment-specific data provisions were found in this or subsequent searches. Code 2 (General Data Protection Legislation, not payment-specific) confirmed.

Definition: Percentage of the adult population (15+ years) who have made at least one digital payment transaction through the instant payment system in the past 90 days, indicating active usage rather than just account ownership.
Comments: Ecofin Agency reports that “about 26% of adults hold an electronic money account” in Guinea (Nov 2025), implying the share of active digital payment users is well under 50%; mapped to <20%? but since e-money account holding is 26%, scored as 20–49% bracket for active digital payment users ([Ecofin Agency](https://www.ecofinagency.com/news-finances/0711-50255-guinea-plans-mobile-payment-system-to-ease-cash-shortage)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed at 20-49% but with a caveat. BCRG's Nov 2025 estimate of ~26% of adults holding an e-money account is corroborated in order of magnitude by a Feb 2026 market report citing 3.2 million active mobile money accounts as of June 2025 (~35-40% of Guinea's ~8.6m adults, allowing for the fact accounts, not unique users, are counted). IMF Financial Access Survey data (FRED, active mobile money accounts per 1,000 adults) shows a higher figure of ~53% for 2024, which would sit in the 50-69% bracket; this is likely inflated by account duplication across the now three licensed e-money providers. Given the direct, most recent BCRG/market statements converge around 26-40%, the 20-49% bracket (code 2) is retained, but the discrepancy with IMF FAS data means this should be treated as a moderate- rather than high-confidence estimate.
